title: Active and passive voice
body:
**Objectives:** identify who performs an action; change active to passive without changing tense; explain when the actor can be omitted.

**Teaching:** In an active sentence, the subject performs the action. A passive sentence makes the receiver the subject. Use the appropriate form of **be** and the main verb's past participle. Keep the original tense. Add **by** and the actor when that information matters. Not every verb has an object that can become a passive subject.

**Worked example:** “The pupils cleaned the classroom.” The action is past; the receiver is the classroom. Therefore: “The classroom was cleaned by the pupils.” “The prefect checks the register” becomes “The register is checked by the prefect.”

**Practice:** Change (1) The gardener waters the plants. (2) Ada repaired the chair. (3) The team will paint the gate. Explain why “The baby sleeps” cannot be changed in the same way.

**Answers:** (1) The plants are watered by the gardener. (2) The chair was repaired by Ada. (3) The gate will be painted by the team. “Sleeps” has no object here.

title: Reflexive and relative pronouns
body:
**Objectives:** distinguish a pronoun referring back to the subject from a pronoun introducing a relative clause; use each in a complete sentence.

**Teaching:** Use a reflexive pronoun when the subject and object refer to the same person or group: “I taught myself the song.” Forms include myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves and themselves. A relative pronoun links a noun to more information: “The pupil who won is smiling.” **Who** commonly refers to people, **which** to things, and **whose** to possession. Do not use a reflexive pronoun simply because it sounds formal.

**Practice:** Complete: (1) We prepared the posters ____. (2) The girl ____ bag was lost reported it. (3) This is the desk ____ needs repair. Explain the function of the added word in each sentence.

**Answers:** ourselves; whose; which/that. The first refers back to “we”; the others introduce relative clauses.

title: Expository essay
body:
**Objectives:** explain a topic clearly; organise an introduction, developed paragraphs and conclusion; distinguish explanation from unsupported opinion.

**Teaching:** An expository essay helps the reader understand a topic or process. State the focus early. Give each body paragraph a clear point, followed by explanation or an example. Arrange a process in its actual sequence. Use connecting words where they clarify relationships. End by bringing the explanation together rather than introducing an unrelated topic.

**Worked plan: How our class keeps its reading corner organised.** Introduction: explain the purpose. Paragraph 1: classify books. Paragraph 2: record borrowing. Paragraph 3: return and check books. Conclusion: explain how the system makes books easy to find.

**Practice:** Write 180–220 words using this plan. Exchange work with a partner, who identifies one clear explanation and one point needing detail.

title: Bookkeeping ethics
body:
**Objectives:** explain transparency, accountability and probity; apply them to a simple class-business record.

**Teaching:** A useful financial record must be understandable and honest. Transparency means making relevant information clear. Accountability means being able to explain and justify how money was handled. Probity means acting with integrity. Keep receipts, record the full amount, explain a correction instead of hiding it, and follow the agreed approval procedure. A record that balances can still be dishonest if a transaction was omitted.

**Scenario:** A class receives ₦8,000 for materials. It spends ₦5,500 and holds ₦2,500. A receipt is missing. The treasurer proposes recording only ₦5,000 spent and keeping ₦500.

**Questions:** What should the record show? Which ethical duties are involved? How should the missing receipt be handled?

**Answers:** Record the actual ₦5,500 expense and ₦2,500 balance. Do not retain ₦500 privately. Explain the missing evidence, seek a duplicate or approved supporting record, and report the discrepancy to the responsible adult.

title: Proofreading and speed development
body:
Objectives: recognise common proof instructions, produce a corrected copy, and record typing speed separately from accuracy.
Teaching: A proof mark tells the typist what to change. Read the mark with the affected text. The accompanying original chart shows caret for insertion, ¶ for a new paragraph, and the textual instructions del, tr, caps, lc and stet. Stet means retain the original wording after a proposed correction is cancelled. House styles vary; use the key supplied for an exercise.
Practice text: 'the reading reading club meets friday. Bring book your. We will share storys.' Instructions: (1) capitalise the first letter; (2) delete the repeated reading; (3) capitalise Friday; (4) transpose book and your; (5) insert a before storys; (6) replace storys with story; (7) begin a new paragraph at We.
Answer: 'The reading club meets Friday. Bring your book.' New paragraph: 'We will share a story.' Award one mark per correctly executed instruction.
Timed practice passage: 'Our reading club meets after school on Friday. Each pupil brings a book and chooses a quiet place to read. After ten minutes we discuss one interesting idea with a partner. We listen carefully and ask questions when a point is unclear. The class secretary records the titles that pupils recommend. Before leaving we return borrowed books to the correct shelf and check the room together. A clear record helps everyone find a suitable book next time. Regular practice improves our reading habits and gives us useful ideas for writing stories, letters and reports for the school magazine each month.'
The passage has 100 whitespace-separated words. Type it twice, recording seconds and uncorrected errors. Gross words per minute = words typed × 60 ÷ seconds. Report errors separately. Worked result: 100 words in 120 seconds gives 50 words per minute; three errors must still be reported. Assessment: compare accuracy first, then speed, and state one change to practise next.

title: Scale drawing
body:
**Objectives:** interpret a ratio scale; convert units before calculation; draw and label a simple shape to scale.

**Teaching:** A scale of 1:50 means one unit on the drawing represents fifty of the same units in reality. Drawing length = actual length ÷ 50. Actual length = drawing length × 50. State the units and scale; do not assume a resized screen image can be measured accurately with a ruler.

**Worked example:** A 4 m wall is 400 cm long. At 1:50 its drawing length is 400 ÷ 50 = 8 cm.

**Practice:** (1) Draw a 6 m × 4 m rectangular room at 1:100. (2) A line measures 3.5 cm on a 1:20 drawing. Find the actual length. (3) Explain why measuring an enlarged phone screenshot gives unreliable results.

**Answers:** (1) 6 cm × 4 cm, with scale and dimensions labelled. (2) 70 cm. (3) Screen resizing changes the relationship between displayed size and original drawing size.

title: Statistics II: averages
body:
**Objectives:** calculate mean, median and mode; explain why they can differ.

**Teaching:** The mean is the sum divided by the number of values. To find the median, put the values in order and find the middle; with an even number of values, average the middle two. The mode is the most frequent value; there may be more than one mode or no unique mode.

**Worked example:** For 2, 4, 4, 5, 10, the sum is 25 and there are five values. Mean = 5; median = 4; mode = 4. The largest value raises the mean.

**Practice:** Find all three averages for (1) 3, 5, 5, 7; (2) 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 7. Explain which values occur most often.

**Answers:** (1) mean 5, median 5, mode 5. (2) mean 3, median 2.5, modes 2 and 3. Award method marks for ordering, summing and identifying frequency.

title: Reading for meaning: facts, opinions and evidence
body:
Objectives: identify the main idea, retrieve details, infer a reason, explain vocabulary in context, and distinguish a checkable statement from a judgement.
Teaching: Skim for the subject and purpose; scan for a specific detail; then read closely. Support an inference with words or actions in the passage. A factual claim can be checked, even when it turns out to be false. An opinion expresses a judgement or preference. Context can suggest a word's meaning; test that meaning in the sentence.
Original practice passage — The reading corner:
On Monday, Sade counted eighteen books in the classroom box. Six had torn covers. She proposed a repair afternoon rather than buying a new box. Musa thought the idea would take too long, but agreed to bring paper and glue. Four pupils repaired the covers on Wednesday. They put a borrowing sheet beside the box and asked readers to record their names. By Friday, nine books had been borrowed and seven returned. Two pupils explained that they had not finished reading. Sade changed the sheet so that it showed an agreed return date. 'This is our best class project,' Musa said. Sade smiled, but decided to count the returned books again the following week before judging whether the new system worked.
Questions: (1) What problem starts the passage? (2) Why add a return date? (3) What does 'proposed' mean here? (4) Give one checkable claim and one opinion. (5) What evidence shows Musa's attitude changed? (6) Give a suitable summary in one sentence.
Answers: Six books have torn covers; the date clarifies when borrowed books are due; suggested; eighteen books were counted/opinion that this is the best project; he first objects then helps and praises it; accept a summary about pupils repairing books and improving borrowing. Distinguish inference from a quotation: Musa's help supports the inference, but does not prove every thought he had.
Assessment: 2 marks each; for inference award one for the explanation and one for supporting evidence. Extension: write a different opinion about the project and label it as your view.

title: Comprehension: the inter-house sports afternoon
body:
Objectives: follow a sequence, infer character, distinguish a result from an opinion, and explain words in context.
Original substitute passage — A different victory:
Blue House had practised the relay for two weeks. On sports afternoon, a short shower left the running surface wet. The games teacher inspected it and delayed the race until it was suitable. During the delay, Tola noticed that a runner from Green House was searching for a missing shoelace. She offered a spare one from her bag. When the race began, Blue House led at the first changeover but finished second. Some classmates complained that helping a rival had distracted Tola. Their captain disagreed: the shoelace had been given away before the race, and every runner had reached the starting line on time. At the assembly, the teacher praised both the winning team and those who had shown consideration for others. Tola still wanted to win the next race. She also wanted every team to have a fair chance.
Questions: (1) Why was the race delayed? (2) Explain 'rival' and 'consideration'. (3) What evidence weakens the complaint against Tola? (4) What position did Blue House finish? (5) State a theme with evidence. (6) Is 'helping always makes you lose' supported?
Answers: A wet surface required inspection/delay; a competitor and thought for others; help was before the race and all were on time; second; fairness/sportsmanship supported by lending the lace; no, one result cannot prove that general claim. Award 2 marks per question for accurate details or reason plus evidence.

title: Comprehension: testing a classroom prediction
body:
Objectives: separate evidence from prediction; identify limitations of a small investigation; infer vocabulary from context.
Original substitute passage — The quiz experiment:
A notice claimed that a computer quiz would make every pupil learn faster. Before accepting the claim, a class tried the quiz with ten volunteers. Each volunteer answered five questions on paper, studied with the quiz for ten minutes, then answered five different questions. Eight scores improved. The organiser announced that the quiz had proved the notice correct. Halima asked whether the second set of questions was easier. She also pointed out that no group had studied for ten minutes without the quiz. The teacher welcomed both the improved scores and Halima's questions. The class decided to compare two similar groups using questions of similar difficulty. They would record results before recommending the quiz to everyone. A useful tool, the teacher explained, should be judged by careful evidence rather than a confident advertisement.
Questions: (1) What is the notice's claim? (2) How many scores improved? (3) Name two weaknesses in the first trial. (4) What does 'volunteers' mean? (5) Does Halima prove the quiz useless? (6) Write a more cautious conclusion.
Answers: Every pupil will learn faster; eight; questions may differ in difficulty and there is no comparison group; people who choose to participate; no, she questions the evidence; accept 'Scores improved for eight volunteers, but a fairer comparison is needed.' Two marks each; question 3 needs both points.

title: Comprehension: a review and its reasons

Objectives: recognise a review, separate plot information from evaluation, and explain how examples support a judgement.
Original substitute passage — Review of a school play:
Our drama club presented The Lost Key on Friday. In the play, a caretaker locks a cupboard containing the prizes for a school ceremony. He then cannot find the key. Three pupils search different places and accuse one another of moving it. The youngest pupil asks everyone to describe what happened in order. title: Narrative writing: planning an event and a short story
body:
Objectives: establish setting and characters; order events; develop a problem and resolution; edit a narrative.

title: Descriptive writing: my favourite subject
body:

title: Writing a debate speech
body:
Objectives: state a position, develop reasons, address a counterargument and use the written form of a speech.
Teaching: A debate speech is written for listeners. Address the chair and audience, state the motion and your position, organise reasons with signposts, consider an opposing argument fairly, and end with a clear conclusion. Each reason needs explanation or an example. Strong language is not a substitute for evidence. In a written task, paragraphs, sentence clarity and punctuation still matter.
Worked opening: 'Chairperson, fellow pupils and guests, I support the proposal that every class should have a reading corner. My first reason is access: a small shared collection lets pupils borrow books between lessons.'
Worked rebuttal: 'Some pupils worry that books will be lost. That is a real concern, but a borrowing record and agreed return dates can help us manage it.' This addresses a concern rather than insulting its supporters.
Practice: Write a 200-word speech for or against 'Our school should hold a weekly reading period'. Include an address, your position, two developed reasons, a counterargument and response, and a concluding appeal. Do not invent statistics. You may use a clearly labelled hypothetical example.
Marking /20: speech form and position 4, reasons/examples 6, fair rebuttal 4, organisation 3, language 3. After feedback, rewrite the rebuttal. Oral delivery can follow, but is not a substitute for the written work.

title: Adverbs of manner and place
body:
Objectives: identify how and where an action occurs and place suitable adverbials in sentences.
Teaching: A manner adverbial answers 'how?'; a place adverbial answers 'where?'. Compare 'Bisi read carefully' with 'Bisi read outside'. Some manner adverbs end in -ly, but not all: 'well' and 'fast' are examples. A phrase such as 'in the library' can also function as a place adverbial. Do not identify a word only by its ending; consider its job in the sentence.
Worked example: 'The pupils waited quietly near the gate.' Quietly tells how; near the gate tells where. Remove either phrase and check which information disappears.
Practice: Identify the adverbials and their kinds in (1) The cat slept upstairs. (2) We carried the tray carefully. (3) They worked well in the classroom. Complete (4) Please speak ____. (5) Put the bag ____. Explain why more than one answer can be acceptable.
Answers: upstairs/place; carefully/manner; well/manner and in the classroom/place; accept clearly/quietly or other meaningful manner; accept here/on the chair or another meaningful place. Sentences 4–5 allow different details provided grammar and meaning fit.
Independent task: describe three actions using both kinds. Mark one point for appropriate meaning and one for grammatical placement in each sentence.

title: Hockey: supervised introductory skills practical
body:
Objectives: demonstrate controlled dribbling, a short push pass and receiving; explain safe spacing and use feedback to improve.
Teacher preparation: inspect the surface and equipment, use suitable protective equipment and a soft practice ball, mark separate lanes, and demonstrate grip and body position. Learners watch the teacher demonstrate each task first, then perform three trials at a comfortable pace. Increase distance only when control and spacing are secure.

title: Taekwondo: supervised non-contact foundation practice
body:
Objectives: follow preparation and stop commands, maintain balance in a basic stance, perform a controlled step and explain respectful non-contact practice.
Preparation: a qualified instructor selects a clear non-slip space, checks suitability for each pupil, and leads a gentle warm-up. Pupils leave enough space for every movement. No partner strikes, sparring, head kicks or board breaking form part of this lesson. Stop for pain, dizziness or loss of safe spacing.
Teaching and practice: the instructor demonstrates an attention position, a respectful bow, a basic ready stance and a short walking stance. Pupils first observe the direction of the feet, posture and balance, then copy the ready position. On command, take one controlled step forward into the demonstrated walking stance, pause in balance, and return. Practise slowly on both sides. The instructor may demonstrate a basic block and a low, controlled kick into empty space; pupils practise only movements the instructor has assessed as suitable and taught directly. This text is a session plan, not a substitute for a movement demonstration.
Assessment: observe response to commands, stable posture, controlled transition, safe spacing and respectful conduct. Score each 0 not yet, 1 with prompts or 2 independently. Give one specific correction, allow a second attempt and record the change. Do not award a belt or claim sparring readiness from this task.
Questions and answers: Why return to a ready stance? To regain balance and prepare for the next instruction. Why is a written quiz insufficient? Movement control must be observed. title: Speech sounds: explicit replacement contrasts
body:
Objectives: distinguish sounds from spellings; recognise schwa and selected consonants; practise contrasts using a pronunciation model.
Teaching: IPA symbols represent sounds. Slashes enclose a pronunciation. The same letter can represent different sounds; use a dictionary's sound recording as well as its spelling. In the British reference model, the first vowel of about is /ə/, the vowel in bird is /ɜː/, and the vowel in cat is /æ/. Schwa commonly occurs in an unstressed syllable. Do not treat the digit 3, letter c or Cyrillic Ә as interchangeable IPA symbols.
Chosen replacement scope: /ɜː/ and /æ/ (bird/bad); /ʒ/ and /dʒ/ (vision/jam); /θ/ and /ð/ (thin/this); /s/ and /z/ (sip/zip); /ʃ/ and /tʃ/ (ship/chip); /w/ and /j/ (wet/yet). Bird/bad and vision/jam are examples of the target sounds, not minimal pairs. For blank source slots these are newly selected contrasts, not recovered author intent.
Practice: use the Cambridge phonetics/pronunciation pages or a competent teacher model. Listen, identify the target sound, repeat, then use each word in a sentence. Touch your throat lightly to notice voicing in /s/ versus /z/; do not force the voice. Compare continuous /ʒ/ with /dʒ/, which begins with a closure and releases into friction.
Written questions: identify the first sound in thin, this, wet and yet; locate schwa in about; explain why a blank source slot cannot prove a particular contrast. Answers: /θ/, /ð/, /w/, /j/; first vowel; it contains no symbol identifying the intended sound.
Assessment: written identification 5 marks; separate listening identification and production observations for each contrast. A written completion does not establish pronunciation accuracy. Respect accent variation and assess the selected reference contrast, not the learner's social background.

title: Informal letter: purpose, structure and tone
body:
Objectives: write a personal letter with an appropriate opening, organised news and a suitable closing.
Teaching: Write for a named person you know. A school letter exercise commonly places the writer's address and date above the salutation. Use paragraphs for separate points, a friendly tone, and a personal closing followed by your name. An email has different address/date fields; do not mechanically copy an email screen into a paper-letter format.
Original model structure: writer's address; date; 'Dear Kemi,'; opening asking after the reader; paragraph describing the reading club; paragraph inviting the friend to visit; 'Best wishes,'; writer's name. In the body, explain details the recipient needs rather than assuming they know your school timetable.
Practice: Write 180 words to a friend about a new school activity. State what happens, when it meets, why you enjoy it and what you would like your friend to do. Use a fictional address for classroom work; do not publish your home address in a shared exercise.
Assessment /20: appropriate format 4; relevant developed content 6; clear paragraphs 4; friendly consistent tone 3; language 3. Answers vary, but an invitation without a time or purpose needs revision. Compare your result with the existing formal-letter lesson: identify a difference in salutation, closing and tone. Preserve the original school lesson's location; this supplementary task supplies a clear First-Term practice point.

title: Article writing and paragraph structure
body:
Objectives: write for a defined audience; build a focused paragraph; connect an introduction, body and conclusion.
Teaching: An article has a purpose and intended readers. Choose a title that signals the topic. Introduce the issue, develop one main point per paragraph and finish with a relevant conclusion. A useful paragraph contains a point, explanation and example; these are functions, not a rule that every paragraph must have exactly three sentences.
Original model paragraph: 'Clear labels save time in a shared store. When every shelf names the items it holds, pupils can return equipment without asking someone else. In our class, separate labels for rulers and pencils stopped the two boxes being mixed up.' The first sentence states the point; the next explains it; the last illustrates it.
Practice: Write a 180–220-word article for the school magazine entitled 'Making our classroom easier to use'. Plan an introduction, two developed suggestions and a conclusion. Use realistic examples rather than invented survey results. Label the point, explanation and example in one body paragraph.
Assessment /20: audience/title 3; relevant ideas 5; paragraph development 5; connections/conclusion 4; language 3. Peer feedback must name one effective example and one unsupported statement. Revise that statement by explaining it or removing it. This lesson supplies a defined structure-writing exercise; it does not claim that the source's vague heading specified a particular missing page.

title: Rhyme scheme and poetic meaning
body:
Objectives: identify end rhyme by sound, label a rhyme scheme, and connect imagery to meaning.
Original teaching poem — After the rain:
The rain has washed the dusty street,
A shining pool reflects the light;
We step around it on our feet,
And watch the clouds turn silver-white.

Teaching: Read the poem aloud. Compare the final stressed sounds, not only the spelling. Street and feet rhyme; light and white rhyme. Give the first ending A, the next different ending B, and reuse a letter when its rhyme returns: ABAB. A rhyme scheme describes the pattern; it does not explain the whole poem. Imagery invites the reader to picture or sense something.
Questions: (1) Write the scheme. (2) Name each rhyming pair. (3) What image suggests reflection? (4) Explain why light and white rhyme despite their different spellings. (5) Is 'rain is always pleasant' proved by the poem?
Answers: ABAB; street/feet and light/white; the shining pool reflecting light; their ending sounds agree; no, the poem presents one imagined scene. Award 2 marks each.
Practice: Write a four-line stanza with either AABB or ABAB, label its ending sounds, and explain one image. Do not sacrifice sense just to force a rhyme. The poem is newly authored, so the full text and questions are available without a missing textbook page. It is not attributed to William Blake or any other poet.

title: Àkànlò èdè: meaning in context
body:
Objectives: distinguish literal wording from an idiomatic meaning and select an expression that fits a situation.
Teaching: Àkànlò èdè is an established expression whose intended meaning is not obtained by translating each word separately. Context helps a listener choose the intended meaning. It can express an idea briefly, but an unfamiliar listener may misunderstand it. Do not invent an expression and call it a traditional idiom.
Source examples, retaining the reference's unmarked spelling: 'o fori gbota' — encountered misfortune; 'o faraya' — became very angry; 'na papa bora' — fled. These short expressions are quoted from the listed lesson; the explanations and practice below are newly prepared.
Practice: (1) A character escapes when trouble starts: choose the expression matching the action. (2) A character becomes extremely angry: choose the matching expression. (3) Explain why a literal word-by-word translation could confuse a learner. (4) Write a short Yoruba sentence around one expression, then explain its intended meaning in context.
Answers: na papa bora; o faraya; an idiom carries a conventional meaning beyond the separate words; accept a sentence whose context supports the supplied meaning. Do not assess a new sentence as a historical quotation.
Assessment: 2 marks for each matching answer; 2 for the explanation; 4 for a meaningful contextual sentence and explanation. For oral practice, the teacher models pronunciation and learners repeat in context. title: Gbólóhùn oníbọ̀: linking a clause to another clause
body:
Objectives: recognise a clause embedded in another construction and use an appropriate linking word.
Teaching: A complex sentence can contain a clause that depends on or adds information to another clause. Yoruba markers such as ti, pé, bí and nígbà help express relationships; the meaning depends on the sentence, so a marker is not a complete analysis by itself. Compare a statement with an added description or condition.
Original examples: 'Mo rí ọmọ náà.' Then 'Mo rí ọmọ tí ó ra ìwé náà.' The added words identify the child. 'A ó lọ bí òjò bá dá.' The added clause states a condition for going. Read the whole sentence before deciding what each part contributes.
Practice: (1) In 'Mo rí ọmọ tí ó ra ìwé náà', identify the clause describing the child. (2) In 'A ó lọ bí òjò bá dá', identify the condition. (3) Join two short ideas using ti, then explain what the new clause tells the reader. (4) Explain why removing a dependent clause may remove important information.
Answers: tí ó ra ìwé náà; bí òjò bá dá; accept a grammatical relative construction with a clear antecedent; the clause may identify a person or give a condition. Assess the relationship and complete meaning, not simply the presence of ti.
Assessment: identification 4 marks; original sentence 4; explanation 2. The teacher reads the examples and checks tone and meaning during oral practice. This supplement covers the grammar strand only; it does not by itself close the entire multi-strand Week 5 literature entry.

title: Ọ̀rọ̀ àpọ́nlé: recognising how an action is described
body:
Objectives: identify a word that adds information to an action or description and explain its contribution.
Teaching: Ọ̀rọ̀ àpọ́nlé adds detail to a predicate, for example manner or degree. Read the word in its sentence rather than treating every vivid word as an adverb. Compare a sentence with and without the added detail and explain the difference.
Source example: 'Olu sare tete'. The final word adds information to the action. The reference also illustrates vivid modifiers, but this exercise concentrates on recognising their function rather than memorising a long list.
Original practice: Read 'Adé rìn díẹ̀díẹ̀' and 'Bísí sọ̀rọ̀ kedere'. Identify the expression that tells how the action happens. Remove it and describe which information has disappeared. Write a new sentence using one of those expressions, keeping a clear subject and action.
Answers: díẹ̀díẹ̀ and kedere; the first loses the gradual manner, the second loses clarity of speech. Accept another meaningful sentence showing the same function. Explain the answer in Yoruba or in a short bilingual gloss, but retain the Yoruba example for analysis.
Assessment: 2 marks for each identification, 2 for each explanation, and 2 for an appropriate original sentence. Oral extension: teacher models the complete sentences and learners repeat with attention to tone. title: Prose study: The Gift of the Magi
body:
Objectives: identify setting, character, plot and theme; explain an ironic ending using evidence.
Selected substitute: O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi (1905), complete public-domain story supplied below and linked in the references. The following is a short teaching synopsis, not the author's text or the school's unidentified prescribed book.
Synopsis: Della and Jim have little money but each wants to buy the other a special Christmas gift. Della sells her long hair to buy a chain for Jim's treasured watch. Jim sells that watch to buy combs for Della's hair. Their presents cannot immediately be used as intended, yet both sacrifices show affection. The unexpected matching sacrifices create the ending's irony.
Teaching: Plot is the connected sequence of events; characterisation shows what a person is like through actions, speech and description. A theme is an idea developed through the story, not simply its topic. Explain a theme such as generosity with an action supporting it. An ironic outcome differs meaningfully from what a character expects.
Study sequence: session 1 read the complete story below and list the starting problem, decisions and outcome; session 2 compare Jim and Della, citing an action by each; session 3 analyse the ending and write a supported paragraph. Use the synopsis for orientation, not as a substitute for reading the complete work.
Questions: What does each character give up? Why can the gifts not be used at once? Does the ending show that the gifts have no value at all? Distinguish material usefulness from emotional meaning.
Answers: Hair and watch respectively; the objects for which the presents were bought are gone; accept a reasoned distinction supported by both sacrifices. Mark factual accuracy 4, explanation of irony 4, evidence-based interpretation 4. Do not require agreement with one moral judgement if the argument fits the text.
Second-Term revision: create a plot timeline from memory, check it against the story, and improve a paragraph after feedback. Record author and title accurately.

COMPLETE READING TEXT — O. Henry, The Gift of the Magi
The Gift of the Magi

by O. Henry


One dollar and eighty-seven cents. That was all. And sixty cents of it
was in pennies. Pennies saved one and two at a time by bulldozing the
grocer and the vegetable man and the butcher until one’s cheeks burned
with the silent imputation of parsimony that such close dealing
implied. Three times Della counted it. One dollar and eighty-seven
cents. And the next day would be Christmas.

There was clearly nothing to do but flop down on the shabby little
couch and howl. So Della did it. Which instigates the moral reflection
that life is made up of sobs, sniffles, and smiles, with sniffles
predominating.

While the mistress of the home is gradually subsiding from the first
stage to the second, take a look at the home. A furnished flat at $8
per week. It did not exactly beggar description, but it certainly had
that word on the lookout for the mendicancy squad.

In the vestibule below was a letter-box into which no letter would go,
and an electric button from which no mortal finger could coax a ring.
Also appertaining thereunto was a card bearing the name “Mr. James
Dillingham Young.”

The “Dillingham” had been flung to the breeze during a former period of
prosperity when its possessor was being paid $30 per week. Now, when
the income was shrunk to $20, though, they were thinking seriously of
contracting to a modest and unassuming D. But whenever Mr. James
Dillingham Young came home and reached his flat above he was called
“Jim” and greatly hugged by Mrs. James Dillingham Young, already
introduced to you as Della. Which is all very good.

Della finished her cry and attended to her cheeks with the powder rag.
She stood by the window and looked out dully at a gray cat walking a
gray fence in a gray backyard. Tomorrow would be Christmas Day, and she
had only $1.87 with which to buy Jim a present. She had been saving
every penny she could for months, with this result. Twenty dollars a
week doesn’t go far. Expenses had been greater than she had calculated.
They always are. Only $1.87 to buy a present for Jim. Her Jim. Many a
happy hour she had spent planning for something nice for him. Something
fine and rare and sterling—something just a little bit near to being
worthy of the honor of being owned by Jim.

There was a pier glass between the windows of the room. Perhaps you
have seen a pier glass in an $8 flat. A very thin and very agile person
may, by observing his reflection in a rapid sequence of longitudinal
strips, obtain a fairly accurate conception of his looks. Della, being
slender, had mastered the art.

Suddenly she whirled from the window and stood before the glass. Her
eyes were shining brilliantly, but her face had lost its color within
twenty seconds. Rapidly she pulled down her hair and let it fall to its
full length.

Now, there were two possessions of the James Dillingham Youngs in which
they both took a mighty pride. One was Jim’s gold watch that had been
his father’s and his grandfather’s. The other was Della’s hair. Had the
queen of Sheba lived in the flat across the airshaft, Della would have
let her hair hang out the window some day to dry just to depreciate Her
Majesty’s jewels and gifts. Had King Solomon been the janitor, with all
his treasures piled up in the basement, Jim would have pulled out his
watch every time he passed, just to see him pluck at his beard from
envy.

So now Della’s beautiful hair fell about her rippling and shining like
a cascade of brown waters. It reached below her knee and made itself
almost a garment for her. And then she did it up again nervously and
quickly. Once she faltered for a minute and stood still while a tear or
two splashed on the worn red carpet.

On went her old brown jacket; on went her old brown hat. With a whirl
of skirts and with the brilliant sparkle still in her eyes, she
fluttered out the door and down the stairs to the street.

Where she stopped the sign read: “Mme. Sofronie. Hair Goods of All
Kinds.” One flight up Della ran, and collected herself, panting.
Madame, large, too white, chilly, hardly looked the “Sofronie.”

“Will you buy my hair?” asked Della.

“I buy hair,” said Madame. “Take yer hat off and let’s have a sight at
the looks of it.”

Down rippled the brown cascade.

“Twenty dollars,” said Madame, lifting the mass with a practised hand.

“Give it to me quick,” said Della.

Oh, and the next two hours tripped by on rosy wings. Forget the hashed
metaphor. She was ransacking the stores for Jim’s present.

She found it at last. It surely had been made for Jim and no one else.
There was no other like it in any of the stores, and she had turned all
of them inside out. It was a platinum fob chain simple and chaste in
design, properly proclaiming its value by substance alone and not by
meretricious ornamentation—as all good things should do. It was even
worthy of The Watch. As soon as she saw it she knew that it must be
Jim’s. It was like him. Quietness and value—the description applied to
both. Twenty-one dollars they took from her for it, and she hurried
home with the 87 cents. With that chain on his watch Jim might be
properly anxious about the time in any company. Grand as the watch was,
he sometimes looked at it on the sly on account of the old leather
strap that he used in place of a chain.

When Della reached home her intoxication gave way a little to prudence
and reason. She got out her curling irons and lighted the gas and went
to work repairing the ravages made by generosity added to love. Which
is always a tremendous task, dear friends—a mammoth task.

Within forty minutes her head was covered with tiny, close-lying curls
that made her look wonderfully like a truant schoolboy. She looked at
her reflection in the mirror long, carefully, and critically.

“If Jim doesn’t kill me,” she said to herself, “before he takes a
second look at me, he’ll say I look like a Coney Island chorus girl.
But what could I do—oh! what could I do with a dollar and eighty-seven
cents?”

At 7 o’clock the coffee was made and the frying-pan was on the back of
the stove hot and ready to cook the chops.

Jim was never late. Della doubled the fob chain in her hand and sat on
the corner of the table near the door that he always entered. Then she
heard his step on the stair away down on the first flight, and she
turned white for just a moment. She had a habit of saying a little
silent prayer about the simplest everyday things, and now she
whispered: “Please God, make him think I am still pretty.”

The door opened and Jim stepped in and closed it. He looked thin and
very serious. Poor fellow, he was only twenty-two—and to be burdened
with a family! He needed a new overcoat and he was without gloves.

Jim stopped inside the door, as immovable as a setter at the scent of
quail. His eyes were fixed upon Della, and there was an expression in
them that she could not read, and it terrified her. It was not anger,
nor surprise, nor disapproval, nor horror, nor any of the sentiments
that she had been prepared for. He simply stared at her fixedly with
that peculiar expression on his face.

Della wriggled off the table and went for him.

“Jim, darling,” she cried, “don’t look at me that way. I had my hair
cut off and sold because I couldn’t have lived through Christmas
without giving you a present. It’ll grow out again—you won’t mind, will
you? I just had to do it. My hair grows awfully fast. Say ‘Merry
Christmas!’ Jim, and let’s be happy. You don’t know what a nice—what a
beautiful, nice gift I’ve got for you.”

“You’ve cut off your hair?” asked Jim, laboriously, as if he had not
arrived at that patent fact yet even after the hardest mental labor.

“Cut it off and sold it,” said Della. “Don’t you like me just as well,
anyhow? I’m me without my hair, ain’t I?”

Jim looked about the room curiously.

“You say your hair is gone?” he said, with an air almost of idiocy.

“You needn’t look for it,” said Della. “It’s sold, I tell you—sold and
gone, too. It’s Christmas Eve, boy. Be good to me, for it went for you.
Maybe the hairs of my head were numbered,” she went on with sudden
serious sweetness, “but nobody could ever count my love for you. Shall
I put the chops on, Jim?”

Out of his trance Jim seemed quickly to wake. He enfolded his Della.
For ten seconds let us regard with discreet scrutiny some
inconsequential object in the other direction. Eight dollars a week or
a million a year—what is the difference? A mathematician or a wit would
give you the wrong answer. The magi brought valuable gifts, but that
was not among them. This dark assertion will be illuminated later on.

Jim drew a package from his overcoat pocket and threw it upon the
table.

“Don’t make any mistake, Dell,” he said, “about me. I don’t think
there’s anything in the way of a haircut or a shave or a shampoo that
could make me like my girl any less. But if you’ll unwrap that package
you may see why you had me going a while at first.”

White fingers and nimble tore at the string and paper. And then an
ecstatic scream of joy; and then, alas! a quick feminine change to
hysterical tears and wails, necessitating the immediate employment of
all the comforting powers of the lord of the flat.

For there lay The Combs—the set of combs, side and back, that Della had
worshipped long in a Broadway window. Beautiful combs, pure tortoise
shell, with jewelled rims—just the shade to wear in the beautiful
vanished hair. They were expensive combs, she knew, and her heart had
simply craved and yearned over them without the least hope of
possession. And now, they were hers, but the tresses that should have
adorned the coveted adornments were gone.

But she hugged them to her bosom, and at length she was able to look up
with dim eyes and a smile and say: “My hair grows so fast, Jim!”

And then Della leaped up like a little singed cat and cried, “Oh, oh!”

Jim had not yet seen his beautiful present. She held it out to him
eagerly upon her open palm. The dull precious metal seemed to flash
with a reflection of her bright and ardent spirit.

“Isn’t it a dandy, Jim? I hunted all over town to find it. You’ll have
to look at the time a hundred times a day now. Give me your watch. I
want to see how it looks on it.”

Instead of obeying, Jim tumbled down on the couch and put his hands
under the back of his head and smiled.

“Dell,” said he, “let’s put our Christmas presents away and keep ’em a
while. They’re too nice to use just at present. I sold the watch to get
the money to buy your combs. And now suppose you put the chops on.”

The magi, as you know, were wise men—wonderfully wise men—who brought
gifts to the Babe in the manger. They invented the art of giving
Christmas presents. Being wise, their gifts were no doubt wise ones,
possibly bearing the privilege of exchange in case of duplication. And
here I have lamely related to you the uneventful chronicle of two
foolish children in a flat who most unwisely sacrificed for each other
the greatest treasures of their house. But in a last word to the wise
of these days let it be said that of all who give gifts these two were
the wisest. Of all who give and receive gifts, such as they are wisest.
Everywhere they are wisest. They are the magi.

title: Drama study: The Proposal
body:
Objectives: identify the setting, characters, conflict and stage directions; connect comic action to a theme.
Selected substitute: Anton Chekhov, The Proposal, in Plays, Second Series, translated by Julius West. The complete play is supplied below and linked in the references; the lesson selects this work explicitly and does not pretend it is the unidentified school-prescribed play.
Teaching synopsis: Lomov visits Chubukov intending to propose marriage to Natalya. Instead of completing the proposal calmly, he and Natalya quarrel about land and later about their dogs. Chubukov becomes involved. Even the agreement to marry does not remove their readiness to argue. The conflict between the purpose of the visit and the repeated quarrels creates comedy and invites discussion of pride and social expectations.
Teaching: Drama presents action through dialogue and performance. Stage directions describe actions or delivery; they are not words every actor should speak aloud. Setting includes place and circumstances. Characterisation can be inferred from repeated behaviour, but a claim about a character needs evidence from the play.
Study sequence: session 1 read the cast, opening and land dispute; session 2 read the return, dog dispute and ending; session 3 rehearse a short exchange, explain a direction and compare the outcome with the original purpose of the visit. Read insults as features of the characters, not acceptable classroom behaviour.
Questions: Where does the play take place? Why does Lomov visit? How does the land dispute delay his purpose? Give one action showing pride. Does the ending resolve every disagreement?
Answers: Chubukov's country-house drawing-room; to propose marriage; the characters turn to competing ownership claims; accept a supported example of insisting on superiority or refusing to yield; no, agreement to marry coexists with further argument. Mark accurate detail 4, evidence 4, interpretation 4.
Revision task: compare one theme with The Gift of the Magi. Explain one difference between narrative prose and a dramatic script. Answers should discuss how each work presents action and use an example, not claim all prose or all drama has identical themes.

COMPLETE READING TEXT — Anton Chekhov, The Proposal; translated by Julius West
THE PROPOSAL


CHARACTERS

     STEPAN STEPANOVITCH CHUBUKOV, a landowner
     NATALYA STEPANOVNA, his daughter, twenty-five years old
     IVAN VASSILEVITCH LOMOV, a neighbour of Chubukov, a large and
     hearty, but very suspicious landowner

The scene is laid at CHUBUKOV’s country-house


A drawing-room in CHUBUKOV’S house.

[LOMOV enters, wearing a dress-jacket and white gloves. CHUBUKOV rises
to meet him.]

CHUBUKOV. My dear fellow, whom do I see! Ivan Vassilevitch! I am
extremely glad! [Squeezes his hand] Now this is a surprise, my
darling... How are you?

LOMOV. Thank you. And how may you be getting on?

CHUBUKOV. We just get along somehow, my angel, to your prayers, and
so on. Sit down, please do.... Now, you know, you shouldn’t forget all
about your neighbours, my darling. My dear fellow, why are you so formal
in your get-up? Evening dress, gloves, and so on. Can you be going
anywhere, my treasure?

LOMOV. No, I’ve come only to see you, honoured Stepan Stepanovitch.

CHUBUKOV. Then why are you in evening dress, my precious? As if you’re
paying a New Year’s Eve visit!

LOMOV. Well, you see, it’s like this. [Takes his arm] I’ve come to you,
honoured Stepan Stepanovitch, to trouble you with a request. Not once or
twice have I already had the privilege of applying to you for help, and
you have always, so to speak... I must ask your pardon, I am getting
excited. I shall drink some water, honoured Stepan Stepanovitch.
[Drinks.]

CHUBUKOV. [Aside] He’s come to borrow money! Shan’t give him any!
[Aloud] What is it, my beauty?

LOMOV. You see, Honour Stepanitch... I beg pardon, Stepan Honouritch...
I mean, I’m awfully excited, as you will please notice.... In short, you
alone can help me, though I don’t deserve it, of course... and haven’t
any right to count on your assistance....

CHUBUKOV. Oh, don’t go round and round it, darling! Spit it out! Well?

LOMOV. One moment... this very minute. The fact is, I’ve come to ask the
hand of your daughter, Natalya Stepanovna, in marriage.

CHUBUKOV. [Joyfully] By Jove! Ivan Vassilevitch! Say it again--I didn’t
hear it all!

LOMOV. I have the honour to ask...

CHUBUKOV. [Interrupting] My dear fellow... I’m so glad, and so on....
Yes, indeed, and all that sort of thing. [Embraces and kisses LOMOV]
I’ve been hoping for it for a long time. It’s been my continual desire.
[Sheds a tear] And I’ve always loved you, my angel, as if you were my
own son. May God give you both His help and His love and so on, and I
did so much hope... What am I behaving in this idiotic way for? I’m off
my balance with joy, absolutely off my balance! Oh, with all my soul...
I’ll go and call Natasha, and all that.

LOMOV. [Greatly moved] Honoured Stepan Stepanovitch, do you think I may
count on her consent?

CHUBUKOV. Why, of course, my darling, and... as if she won’t consent!
She’s in love; egad, she’s like a love-sick cat, and so on.... Shan’t be
long! [Exit.]

LOMOV. It’s cold... I’m trembling all over, just as if I’d got an
examination before me. The great thing is, I must have my mind made up.
If I give myself time to think, to hesitate, to talk a lot, to look for
an ideal, or for real love, then I’ll never get married.... Brr!... It’s
cold! Natalya Stepanovna is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking,
well-educated.... What more do I want? But I’m getting a noise in
my ears from excitement. [Drinks] And it’s impossible for me not to
marry.... In the first place, I’m already 35--a critical age, so to
speak. In the second place, I ought to lead a quiet and regular life....
I suffer from palpitations, I’m excitable and always getting awfully
upset.... At this very moment my lips are trembling, and there’s a
twitch in my right eyebrow.... But the very worst of all is the way
I sleep. I no sooner get into bed and begin to go off when suddenly
something in my left side--gives a pull, and I can feel it in my
shoulder and head.... I jump up like a lunatic, walk about a bit, and
lie down again, but as soon as I begin to get off to sleep there’s
another pull! And this may happen twenty times....

[NATALYA STEPANOVNA comes in.]

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Well, there! It’s you, and papa said, “Go; there’s a
merchant come for his goods.” How do you do, Ivan Vassilevitch!

LOMOV. How do you do, honoured Natalya Stepanovna?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. You must excuse my apron and négligé... we’re
shelling peas for drying. Why haven’t you been here for such a long
time? Sit down. [They seat themselves] Won’t you have some lunch?

LOMOV. No, thank you, I’ve had some already.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Then smoke.... Here are the matches.... The weather
is splendid now, but yesterday it was so wet that the workmen didn’t
do anything all day. How much hay have you stacked? Just think, I felt
greedy and had a whole field cut, and now I’m not at all pleased about
it because I’m afraid my hay may rot. I ought to have waited a bit. But
what’s this? Why, you’re in evening dress! Well, I never! Are you going
to a ball, or what?--though I must say you look better. Tell me, why are
you got up like that?

LOMOV. [Excited] You see, honoured Natalya Stepanovna... the fact is,
I’ve made up my mind to ask you to hear me out.... Of course you’ll be
surprised and perhaps even angry, but a... [Aside] It’s awfully cold!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What’s the matter? [Pause] Well?

LOMOV. I shall try to be brief. You must know, honoured Natalya
Stepanovna, that I have long, since my childhood, in fact, had the
privilege of knowing your family. My late aunt and her husband, from
whom, as you know, I inherited my land, always had the greatest respect
for your father and your late mother. The Lomovs and the Chubukovs
have always had the most friendly, and I might almost say the most
affectionate, regard for each other. And, as you know, my land is a near
neighbour of yours. You will remember that my Oxen Meadows touch your
birchwoods.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Excuse my interrupting you. You say, “my Oxen
Meadows....” But are they yours?

LOMOV. Yes, mine.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What are you talking about? Oxen Meadows are ours,
not yours!

LOMOV. No, mine, honoured Natalya Stepanovna.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Well, I never knew that before. How do you make that
out?

LOMOV. How? I’m speaking of those Oxen Meadows which are wedged in
between your birchwoods and the Burnt Marsh.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Yes, yes.... They’re ours.

LOMOV. No, you’re mistaken, honoured Natalya Stepanovna, they’re mine.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Just think, Ivan Vassilevitch! How long have they
been yours?

LOMOV. How long? As long as I can remember.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Really, you won’t get me to believe that!

LOMOV. But you can see from the documents, honoured Natalya Stepanovna.
Oxen Meadows, it’s true, were once the subject of dispute, but now
everybody knows that they are mine. There’s nothing to argue about.
You see, my aunt’s grandmother gave the free use of these Meadows in
perpetuity to the peasants of your father’s grandfather, in return for
which they were to make bricks for her. The peasants belonging to your
father’s grandfather had the free use of the Meadows for forty years,
and had got into the habit of regarding them as their own, when it
happened that...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. No, it isn’t at all like that! Both my grandfather
and great-grandfather reckoned that their land extended to Burnt
Marsh--which means that Oxen Meadows were ours. I don’t see what there
is to argue about. It’s simply silly!

LOMOV. I’ll show you the documents, Natalya Stepanovna!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. No, you’re simply joking, or making fun of me....
What a surprise! We’ve had the land for nearly three hundred years, and
then we’re suddenly told that it isn’t ours! Ivan Vassilevitch, I can
hardly believe my own ears.... These Meadows aren’t worth much to me.
They only come to five dessiatins [Note: 13.5 acres], and are worth
perhaps 300 roubles [Note: £30.], but I can’t stand unfairness. Say what
you will, but I can’t stand unfairness.

LOMOV. Hear me out, I implore you! The peasants of your father’s
grandfather, as I have already had the honour of explaining to you, used
to bake bricks for my aunt’s grandmother. Now my aunt’s grandmother,
wishing to make them a pleasant...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I can’t make head or tail of all this about aunts
and grandfathers and grandmothers! The Meadows are ours, and that’s all.

LOMOV. Mine.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Ours! You can go on proving it for two days on end,
you can go and put on fifteen dress-jackets, but I tell you they’re
ours, ours, ours! I don’t want anything of yours and I don’t want to
give up anything of mine. So there!

LOMOV. Natalya Ivanovna, I don’t want the Meadows, but I am acting on
principle. If you like, I’ll make you a present of them.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I can make you a present of them myself, because
they’re mine! Your behaviour, Ivan Vassilevitch, is strange, to say the
least! Up to this we have always thought of you as a good neighbour, a
friend: last year we lent you our threshing-machine, although on that
account we had to put off our own threshing till November, but you
behave to us as if we were gipsies. Giving me my own land, indeed!
No, really, that’s not at all neighbourly! In my opinion, it’s even
impudent, if you want to know....

LOMOV. Then you make out that I’m a land-grabber? Madam, never in my
life have I grabbed anybody else’s land, and I shan’t allow anybody to
accuse me of having done so.... [Quickly steps to the carafe and drinks
more water] Oxen Meadows are mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true, they’re ours!

LOMOV. Mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true! I’ll prove it! I’ll send my mowers
out to the Meadows this very day!

LOMOV. What?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. My mowers will be there this very day!

LOMOV. I’ll give it to them in the neck!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. You dare!

LOMOV. [Clutches at his heart] Oxen Meadows are mine! You understand?
Mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Please don’t shout! You can shout yourself hoarse in
your own house, but here I must ask you to restrain yourself!

LOMOV. If it wasn’t, madam, for this awful, excruciating palpitation,
if my whole inside wasn’t upset, I’d talk to you in a different way!
[Yells] Oxen Meadows are mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Ours!

LOMOV. Mine!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Ours!

LOMOV. Mine!

[Enter CHUBUKOV.]

CHUBUKOV. What’s the matter? What are you shouting at?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa, please tell to this gentleman who owns Oxen
Meadows, we or he?

CHUBUKOV. [To LOMOV] Darling, the Meadows are ours!

LOMOV. But, please, Stepan Stepanitch, how can they be yours? Do be a
reasonable man! My aunt’s grandmother gave the Meadows for the temporary
and free use of your grandfather’s peasants. The peasants used the land
for forty years and got as accustomed to it as if it was their own, when
it happened that...

CHUBUKOV. Excuse me, my precious.... You forget just this, that the
peasants didn’t pay your grandmother and all that, because the Meadows
were in dispute, and so on. And now everybody knows that they’re ours.
It means that you haven’t seen the plan.

LOMOV. I’ll prove to you that they’re mine!

CHUBUKOV. You won’t prove it, my darling.

LOMOV. I shall!

CHUBUKOV. Dear one, why yell like that? You won’t prove anything just
by yelling. I don’t want anything of yours, and don’t intend to give up
what I have. Why should I? And you know, my beloved, that if you propose
to go on arguing about it, I’d much sooner give up the meadows to the
peasants than to you. There!

LOMOV. I don’t understand! How have you the right to give away somebody
else’s property?

CHUBUKOV. You may take it that I know whether I have the right or not.
Because, young man, I’m not used to being spoken to in that tone of
voice, and so on: I, young man, am twice your age, and ask you to speak
to me without agitating yourself, and all that.

LOMOV. No, you just think I’m a fool and want to have me on! You call
my land yours, and then you want me to talk to you calmly and politely!
Good neighbours don’t behave like that, Stepan Stepanitch! You’re not a
neighbour, you’re a grabber!

CHUBUKOV. What’s that? What did you say?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa, send the mowers out to the Meadows at once!

CHUBUKOV. What did you say, sir?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Oxen Meadows are ours, and I shan’t give them up,
shan’t give them up, shan’t give them up!

LOMOV. We’ll see! I’ll have the matter taken to court, and then I’ll
show you!

CHUBUKOV. To court? You can take it to court, and all that! You can! I
know you; you’re just on the look-out for a chance to go to court, and
all that.... You pettifogger! All your people were like that! All of
them!

LOMOV. Never mind about my people! The Lomovs have all been honourable
people, and not one has ever been tried for embezzlement, like your
grandfather!

CHUBUKOV. You Lomovs have had lunacy in your family, all of you!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. All, all, all!

CHUBUKOV. Your grandfather was a drunkard, and your younger aunt,
Nastasya Mihailovna, ran away with an architect, and so on.

LOMOV. And your mother was hump-backed. [Clutches at his heart]
Something pulling in my side.... My head.... Help! Water!

CHUBUKOV. Your father was a guzzling gambler!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. And there haven’t been many backbiters to equal your
aunt!

LOMOV. My left foot has gone to sleep.... You’re an intriguer.... Oh,
my heart!... And it’s an open secret that before the last elections you
bri... I can see stars.... Where’s my hat?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s low! It’s dishonest! It’s mean!

CHUBUKOV. And you’re just a malicious, double-faced intriguer! Yes!

LOMOV. Here’s my hat.... My heart!... Which way? Where’s the door?
Oh!... I think I’m dying.... My foot’s quite numb.... [Goes to the
door.]

CHUBUKOV. [Following him] And don’t set foot in my house again!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Take it to court! We’ll see!

[LOMOV staggers out.]

CHUBUKOV. Devil take him! [Walks about in excitement.]

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What a rascal! What trust can one have in one’s
neighbours after that!

CHUBUKOV. The villain! The scarecrow!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. The monster! First he takes our land and then he has
the impudence to abuse us.

CHUBUKOV. And that blind hen, yes, that turnip-ghost has the confounded
cheek to make a proposal, and so on! What? A proposal!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What proposal?

CHUBUKOV. Why, he came here so as to propose to you.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. To propose? To me? Why didn’t you tell me so before?

CHUBUKOV. So he dresses up in evening clothes. The stuffed sausage! The
wizen-faced frump!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. To propose to me? Ah! [Falls into an easy-chair and
wails] Bring him back! Back! Ah! Bring him here.

CHUBUKOV. Bring whom here?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Quick, quick! I’m ill! Fetch him! [Hysterics.]

CHUBUKOV. What’s that? What’s the matter with you? [Clutches at his
head] Oh, unhappy man that I am! I’ll shoot myself! I’ll hang myself!
We’ve done for her!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I’m dying! Fetch him!

CHUBUKOV. Tfoo! At once. Don’t yell!

[Runs out. A pause. NATALYA STEPANOVNA wails.]

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What have they done to me! Fetch him back! Fetch
him! [A pause.]

[CHUBUKOV runs in.]

CHUBUKOV. He’s coming, and so on, devil take him! Ouf! Talk to him
yourself; I don’t want to....

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Wails] Fetch him!

CHUBUKOV. [Yells] He’s coming, I tell you. Oh, what a burden, Lord,
to be the father of a grown-up daughter! I’ll cut my throat! I will,
indeed! We cursed him, abused him, drove him out, and it’s all you...
you!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. No, it was you!

CHUBUKOV. I tell you it’s not my fault. [LOMOV appears at the door] Now
you talk to him yourself [Exit.]

[LOMOV enters, exhausted.]

LOMOV. My heart’s palpitating awfully.... My foot’s gone to sleep....
There’s something keeps pulling in my side.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Forgive us, Ivan Vassilevitch, we were all a little
heated.... I remember now: Oxen Meadows really are yours.

LOMOV. My heart’s beating awfully.... My Meadows.... My eyebrows are
both twitching....

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. The Meadows are yours, yes, yours.... Do sit
down.... [They sit] We were wrong....

LOMOV. I did it on principle.... My land is worth little to me, but the
principle...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Yes, the principle, just so.... Now let’s talk of
something else.

LOMOV. The more so as I have evidence. My aunt’s grandmother gave the
land to your father’s grandfather’s peasants...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Yes, yes, let that pass.... [Aside] I wish I knew
how to get him started.... [Aloud] Are you going to start shooting soon?

LOMOV. I’m thinking of having a go at the blackcock, honoured Natalya
Stepanovna, after the harvest. Oh, have you heard? Just think, what a
misfortune I’ve had! My dog Guess, whom you know, has gone lame.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What a pity! Why?

LOMOV. I don’t know.... Must have got twisted, or bitten by some other
dog.... [Sighs] My very best dog, to say nothing of the expense. I gave
Mironov 125 roubles for him.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It was too much, Ivan Vassilevitch.

LOMOV. I think it was very cheap. He’s a first-rate dog.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa gave 85 roubles for his Squeezer, and Squeezer
is heaps better than Guess!

LOMOV. Squeezer better than. Guess? What an idea! [Laughs] Squeezer
better than Guess!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Of course he’s better! Of course, Squeezer is
young, he may develop a bit, but on points and pedigree he’s better than
anything that even Volchanetsky has got.

LOMOV. Excuse me, Natalya Stepanovna, but you forget that he is
overshot, and an overshot always means the dog is a bad hunter!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Overshot, is he? The first time I hear it!

LOMOV. I assure you that his lower jaw is shorter than the upper.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Have you measured?

LOMOV. Yes. He’s all right at following, of course, but if you want him
to get hold of anything...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. In the first place, our Squeezer is a thoroughbred
animal, the son of Harness and Chisels, while there’s no getting at
the pedigree of your dog at all.... He’s old and as ugly as a worn-out
cab-horse.

LOMOV. He is old, but I wouldn’t take five Squeezers for him.... Why,
how can you?... Guess is a dog; as for Squeezer, well, it’s too funny to
argue.... Anybody you like has a dog as good as Squeezer... you may find
them under every bush almost. Twenty-five roubles would be a handsome
price to pay for him.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. There’s some demon of contradiction in you to-day,
Ivan Vassilevitch. First you pretend that the Meadows are yours; now,
that Guess is better than Squeezer. I don’t like people who don’t say
what they mean, because you know perfectly well that Squeezer is a
hundred times better than your silly Guess. Why do you want to say it
isn’t?

LOMOV. I see, Natalya Stepanovna, that you consider me either blind or a
fool. You must realize that Squeezer is overshot!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true.

LOMOV. He is!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. It’s not true!

LOMOV. Why shout, madam?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Why talk rot? It’s awful! It’s time your Guess was
shot, and you compare him with Squeezer!

LOMOV. Excuse me; I cannot continue this discussion: my heart is
palpitating.

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I’ve noticed that those hunters argue most who know
least.

LOMOV. Madam, please be silent.... My heart is going to pieces....
[Shouts] Shut up!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I shan’t shut up until you acknowledge that Squeezer
is a hundred times better than your Guess!

LOMOV. A hundred times worse! Be hanged to your Squeezer! His head...
eyes... shoulder...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. There’s no need to hang your silly Guess; he’s
half-dead already!

LOMOV. [Weeps] Shut up! My heart’s bursting!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I shan’t shut up.

[Enter CHUBUKOV.]

CHUBUKOV. What’s the matter now?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Papa, tell us truly, which is the better dog, our
Squeezer or his Guess.

LOMOV. Stepan Stepanovitch, I implore you to tell me just one thing: is
your Squeezer overshot or not? Yes or no?

CHUBUKOV. And suppose he is? What does it matter? He’s the best dog in
the district for all that, and so on.

LOMOV. But isn’t my Guess better? Really, now?

CHUBUKOV. Don’t excite yourself, my precious one.... Allow me.... Your
Guess certainly has his good points.... He’s pure-bred, firm on his
feet, has well-sprung ribs, and all that. But, my dear man, if you want
to know the truth, that dog has two defects: he’s old and he’s short in
the muzzle.

LOMOV. Excuse me, my heart.... Let’s take the facts.... You will
remember that on the Marusinsky hunt my Guess ran neck-and-neck with the
Count’s dog, while your Squeezer was left a whole verst behind.

CHUBUKOV. He got left behind because the Count’s whipper-in hit him with
his whip.

LOMOV. And with good reason. The dogs are running after a fox, when
Squeezer goes and starts worrying a sheep!

CHUBUKOV. It’s not true!... My dear fellow, I’m very liable to lose my
temper, and so, just because of that, let’s stop arguing. You started
because everybody is always jealous of everybody else’s dogs. Yes, we’re
all like that! You too, sir, aren’t blameless! You no sooner notice that
some dog is better than your Guess than you begin with this, that... and
the other... and all that.... I remember everything!

LOMOV. I remember too!

CHUBUKOV. [Teasing him] I remember, too.... What do you remember?

LOMOV. My heart... my foot’s gone to sleep.... I can’t...

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Teasing] My heart.... What sort of a hunter are
you? You ought to go and lie on the kitchen oven and catch blackbeetles,
not go after foxes! My heart!

CHUBUKOV. Yes really, what sort of a hunter are you, anyway? You ought
to sit at home with your palpitations, and not go tracking animals. You
could go hunting, but you only go to argue with people and interfere
with their dogs and so on. Let’s change the subject in case I lose my
temper. You’re not a hunter at all, anyway!

LOMOV. And are you a hunter? You only go hunting to get in with the
Count and to intrigue.... Oh, my heart!... You’re an intriguer!

CHUBUKOV. What? I an intriguer? [Shouts] Shut up!

LOMOV. Intriguer!

CHUBUKOV. Boy! Pup!

LOMOV. Old rat! Jesuit!

CHUBUKOV. Shut up or I’ll shoot you like a partridge! You fool!

LOMOV. Everybody knows that--oh my heart!--your late wife used to beat
you.... My feet... temples... sparks.... I fall, I fall!

CHUBUKOV. And you’re under the slipper of your housekeeper!

LOMOV. There, there, there... my heart’s burst! My shoulder’s come
off.... Where is my shoulder? I die. [Falls into an armchair] A doctor!
[Faints.]

CHUBUKOV. Boy! Milksop! Fool! I’m sick! [Drinks water] Sick!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. What sort of a hunter are you? You can’t even sit on
a horse! [To her father] Papa, what’s the matter with him? Papa! Look,
papa! [Screams] Ivan Vassilevitch! He’s dead!

CHUBUKOV. I’m sick!... I can’t breathe!... Air!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. He’s dead. [Pulls LOMOV’S sleeve] Ivan Vassilevitch!
Ivan Vassilevitch! What have you done to me? He’s dead. [Falls into an
armchair] A doctor, a doctor! [Hysterics.]

CHUBUKOV. Oh!... What is it? What’s the matter?

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Wails] He’s dead... dead!

CHUBUKOV. Who’s dead? [Looks at LOMOV] So he is! My word! Water! A
doctor! [Lifts a tumbler to LOMOV’S mouth] Drink this!... No, he doesn’t
drink.... It means he’s dead, and all that.... I’m the most unhappy of
men! Why don’t I put a bullet into my brain? Why haven’t I cut my throat
yet? What am I waiting for? Give me a knife! Give me a pistol! [LOMOV
moves] He seems to be coming round.... Drink some water! That’s
right....

LOMOV. I see stars... mist.... Where am I?

CHUBUKOV. Hurry up and get married and--well, to the devil with you!
She’s willing! [He puts LOMOV’S hand into his daughter’s] She’s willing
and all that. I give you my blessing and so on. Only leave me in peace!

LOMOV. [Getting up] Eh? What? To whom?

CHUBUKOV. She’s willing! Well? Kiss and be damned to you!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. [Wails] He’s alive... Yes, yes, I’m willing....

CHUBUKOV. Kiss each other!

LOMOV. Eh? Kiss whom? [They kiss] Very nice, too. Excuse me, what’s
it all about? Oh, now I understand... my heart... stars... I’m happy.
Natalya Stepanovna.... [Kisses her hand] My foot’s gone to sleep....

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. I... I’m happy too....

CHUBUKOV. What a weight off my shoulders.... Ouf!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. But... still you will admit now that Guess is worse
than Squeezer.

LOMOV. Better!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Worse!

CHUBUKOV. Well, that’s a way to start your family bliss! Have some
champagne!

LOMOV. He’s better!

NATALYA STEPANOVNA. Worse! worse! worse!

CHUBUKOV. [Trying to shout her down] Champagne! Champagne!

Curtain.

title: Expository reading: understanding drug addiction
body:
Objectives: identify an explanatory text's main idea, distinguish explanation from stigma, and organise an evidence-based paragraph.
Original reading based on NIDA's educational information:
Drug addiction involves difficulty controlling drug use despite harmful consequences. It affects brain function and behaviour and can require continuing treatment and support. It is not explained simply by calling a person weak or bad. Young people's brains are still developing, so avoiding harmful substance use and seeking trustworthy help matter. People can recover. A person who is worried about substance use should speak with a trusted adult and a qualified health professional rather than rely on classmates to diagnose or treat the problem. Medicines should be used only as directed by an appropriate health professional. Respectful support and accurate information are more useful than humiliation.
Questions: (1) What is the main idea? (2) Why is 'just be stronger' an inadequate explanation? (3) Who should advise on treatment? (4) Find a sentence showing that recovery is possible. (5) What makes this exposition rather than a fictional narrative?
Answers: Addiction is a health problem needing accurate understanding and support; it involves changes in brain function/behaviour and difficulty controlling use; a qualified health professional; the sentence stating that people can recover; it explains an issue rather than telling a sequence about invented characters. Award 2 marks each.
Writing: prepare a 150-word explanation entitled 'Why accurate information matters'. Use an introduction, two developed points and a conclusion. Do not invent treatment instructions, statistics or claims about a classmate. Mark focus 3, organisation 3, supported explanation 4, language 3 and respectful accuracy 2. This is an English explanation exercise, not a medical diagnosis or treatment plan.

title: Àkàyé ọlọ́rọ̀ geere: Ìwé tí ó sọnù
body:
Objectives: read a complete Yoruba prose passage, retrieve details, infer a character's reason, and support a moral interpretation with evidence.
Original classroom story — Ìwé tí ó sọnù:
Ní ọjọ́ Ajé, Bísí lọ sí ilé ìkàwé láti dá ìwé tí ó yá padà. Nígbà tí ó ṣí àpò rẹ̀, kò rí ìwé náà. Ó bẹ̀rù pé òun ti sọ ọ́ nù. Adé, ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀, ní kí wọ́n kọ́kọ́ wá a ní kíláàsì. Wọ́n wo orí tábìlì àti abẹ́ àga, ṣùgbọ́n wọn kò rí i. Lẹ́yìn náà, Bísí rántí pé òun fi ìwé náà sínú àpótí nílé kí òjò má bà á jẹ́. Ó sọ fún olùkọ́ ohun tí ó ṣẹlẹ̀. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, ó mú ìwé náà wá, ó sì dá a padà. Olùkọ́ dúpẹ́ lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ fún sísọ òtítọ́. Bísí pinnu pé òun yóò máa ṣàyẹ̀wò àpò òun kí òun tó kúrò nílé.
Ìbéèrè / Questions: (1) Níbo ni Bísí fẹ́ lọ? (2) Kí ló mú kí ó bẹ̀rù? (3) Níbo ni ìwé náà wà? (4) Kí nìdí tí ó fi ìwé náà síbẹ̀? (5) Kí ni a lè kọ́ nínú ìtàn yìí? (6) Ṣe àkótán ìtàn náà ní gbólóhùn méjì.
Ìdáhùn / Answers: Ilé ìkàwé; kò rí ìwé nínú àpò; nínú àpótí nílé; kí òjò má bà á jẹ́; accept honesty/care supported by telling the teacher or checking the bag; summary should retain the missing-book problem and its resolution.
Teaching: Separate a detail stated in the passage from an inference. The teacher models reading with appropriate tones; pupils reread and explain the problem, search and outcome. This is a complete short teaching story, not a recovered prescribed novel.
Assessment: 2 marks each for questions 1–4; 2 for an evidence-based lesson; 4 for a coherent two-sentence summary. Second-Term extension: retell from Adé's viewpoint without changing where the book was found.

title: Ìkọ̀wé àgbọ́sọ: a fixed dictation and correction task
body:
Objectives: listen carefully, write a fixed Yoruba passage, and correct spelling, tone marks and punctuation against the supplied key.
Teacher reading script and answer key:
Bísí lọ sí ilé ìkàwé. Ó fẹ́ dá ìwé tí ó yá padà. Adé ràn án lọ́wọ́ láti wá ìwé náà. Ní ọjọ́ kejì, Bísí mú ìwé náà wá. Olùkọ́ dúpẹ́ lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀ fún sísọ òtítọ́.
Procedure: The teacher reads the complete script once at a natural pace while pupils listen. Read one sentence at a time, repeating each sentence once, with writing time between them. Read the whole script again for checking. Do not show the script during the dictation. Pupils then compare their work with the exact key and correct errors in a different colour.
Practice: group corrections under missing word, spelling, tone mark, underdot, capital letter and punctuation. Explain how an omitted mark can affect a Yoruba word. Read the corrected passage aloud with the teacher's model.
Assessment: score each sentence out of four: two for all words in their intended order, one for correct diacritics, and one for capitals and punctuation. A missing word loses only the appropriate word-accuracy credit; avoid counting it again as several unrelated errors. Total 20. Repeat the weakest sentence after feedback rather than rewarding speed alone.
This is an original fixed script based on the companion classroom story. It supplies the missing dictation exercise; it is not a claim that the school source contained these sentences. An app may show the key after practice, but a text-only quiz does not assess listening.

title: Àkàyé ewì: Ìwé mi
body:
Objectives: read a complete short Yoruba poem, identify imagery and repetition, and explain a theme with evidence.
Original classroom poem — Ìwé mi:
Ìwé mi, ọ̀rẹ́ mi,
Mo ṣí ọ ní òwúrọ̀.
Ọ̀rọ̀ rẹ ń tan ìmọ́lẹ̀,
Ó ń ṣí ọ̀nà fún mi.
Mo ka, mo ronú,
Mo béèrè, mo kọ́.

Teaching: The speaker addresses a book as a friend. Light and a path are images for understanding and discovery; they do not mean that paper literally shines or makes a road. Repeated 'Mo' keeps attention on the learner's actions. A poem need not have an English-style end-rhyme scheme to communicate through rhythm, imagery and repeated structures.
Ìbéèrè / Questions: (1) Kí ni akéwì pè ní ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ̀? (2) Ṣàlàyé 'ìmọ́lẹ̀' nínú ewì yìí. (3) Kọ àwọn iṣẹ́ méjì tí olùsọ̀rọ̀ ń ṣe. (4) Kí ni àtúnwí 'Mo' ń fi hàn? (5) Kí ni kókó ewì náà?
Answers: the book; understanding rather than literal light; any two of reading, thinking, asking and learning; focus on the speaker's active participation; learning through thoughtful reading and questions. Award two marks for each supported answer.
Practice: read the poem with pauses at the line endings, then explain whether every line ending requires a full stop. Write two original Yoruba lines about a useful learning activity. Mark meaningful imagery and clear expression; do not label a newly written poem as traditional oral literature. This complete practice poem replaces an unspecified reading exercise, not an identified government-prescribed work.

title: Àrọkọ alálàyé: explaining a familiar process
body:
Objectives: explain a process in a logical order, use focused paragraphs and revise a Yoruba composition for clarity.
Teaching: Àrọkọ alálàyé explains a subject or how something works. Decide what the reader needs to understand. Introduce the subject, develop the steps or main points, and end with a relevant conclusion. Give enough detail for the explanation to be useful; do not substitute a list of unexplained headings.
Original task: Kọ àrọkọ lórí bí a ṣe ń tọ́jú ìwé ní ilé ìkàwé. Explain how books are kept in good condition and returned to the correct place. Plan: introduction to the library; handling books carefully; recording borrowing and returning books; why the routine helps other readers.
Original opening model: 'Ilé ìkàwé jẹ́ ibi tí a ti ń ka ìwé, tí a sì ti ń kọ́ ẹ̀kọ́. Ó yẹ kí a máa tọ́jú àwọn ìwé kí àwọn mìíràn lè lò wọ́n.' Continue with your own explanation rather than copying the opening repeatedly.
Practice: write 150–200 words in Yoruba. Exchange work with a partner. Ask the partner to identify one clear instruction and one step needing explanation. Rewrite that step.
Assessment /20: relevant content 6; logical sequence and paragraphs 4; developed explanation 4; Yoruba spelling and diacritics 4; relevant conclusion 2. Answers vary, but each recommendation should explain what to do and why. This covers the composition strand only; inheritance and lineage-praise objectives in the same scheme weeks require their own teaching.
